summary: Hebrews 10 (39 verses) continues the story of Jesus greater. Starting with 'For the law, having a shadow of the good to come, not the very image of the things, can never with the same sacrifices year by year, which they offer continuall', it moves through themes of Jesus greater, new covenant and calls readers toward endurance.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows Jesus greater lived out in exhortation. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: For the law, having a shadow of the good to come, not the very image of the things, can never with the same sacrifices year by year, which they offer continually, make perfect those who draw near.
by the way which he dedicated for us, a new and living way, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh,
But we are not of those who shrink back to destruction, but of those who have faith to the saving of the soul.

questions.question: What is happening in Hebrews 10?
questions.answer: In 39 verses, this chapter hebrews 10 (39 verses) continues the story of jesus greater. starting with 'for the law, having a shadow of the good to come, not the very image of the things, can never with the same sacrifices year by year, which they offer continuall', it moves through themes of jesus greater, new covenant and calls readers toward endurance. The setting is exhortation, written to jewish christians tempted to return. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Hebrews and why 10 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally anonymous, pauline circle, addressed to jewish christians tempted to return around ad 60-70. This chapter fits the book's purpose as sermon letter — its themes of Jesus greater, new covenant build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'covenant' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Binding promise/agreement God makes with people. In this chapter, it appears in context of Jesus greater. For a first-time reader: think of it as binding promise/agreement god makes with people, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through Jesus greater and new covenant, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 29 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'How much worse punishment do you think he will be judged worthy of who has trodden under foot the Son of God, and has counted the blood of the covenant with which he was sanctified...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about Jesus greater. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?

glossary.def: Binding promise/agreement God makes with people
